Well, I don't have some big plan or anything like that to hurt myself. But... a lot of mornings, I wake up and just think it might be easier if I didn't wake up at all.

Well, yeah, I do. All the time, really. I keep thinking about how I failed everybody when I lost my old place and just... couldn't keep my life together. It's like this heavy weight, you know? It made this awful grinding noise, sounded like a garbage truck backing up. The repairman who came out to fix it, he had this fascinating theory about how modern appliances are designed to fail after a certain number of years. Planned obsolescence, he called it. He said back in the fifties, they built things to last forever because they used solid steel and copper wiring. Now it's all plastic gears and microchips that fry if the power surges. 

He was actually a really interesting guy. He used to build model airplanes in his spare time. The kind with the tiny little gas engines that you fly with remote controls. He told me he once spent six months building a scale model of a P-51 Mustang, painted the invasion stripes and everything. Did you know the P-51 was originally designed for the British, but it didn't really become famous until they put a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine in it? It completely changed the air war over Europe. 

But... yeah, the guilt. It just sort of sits there in my chest. I just feel like everything that goes wrong is somehow my fault, even when it doesn't make sense.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no... I haven't really noticed myself pacing or feeling fidgety. I'm usually pretty still, to be honest. Mostly I just sit in my chair when I get home. It's one of those recliners, you know, the kind with the lever on the side that always sticks a little bit. I bought it second-hand from a guy who was moving to Florida. He said he couldn't take it with him because the humidity down there ruins upholstery. 

He was actually moving to Sarasota. Did you know Sarasota has some of the finest white sand beaches in the world? It's because the sand is made of pure quartz that washed down from the Appalachian Mountains millions of years ago. It stays cool even in the hot sun because it reflects the light. The guy told me he was going to buy a metal detector and just walk the beaches looking for lost jewelry. People lose so many rings and watches in the water because the cold ocean shrinks their fingers. 

He showed me this old silver coin he found once in a park up here. A Mercury dime, from 1942. They're actually mostly silver, not like the coins we have now. The government stopped making silver coins for regular circulation back in 1964 because the silver was worth more than the face value of the coin. It's funny how value changes like that, isn't it? Something that's just a dime one day is suddenly worth a lot more just because of what it's made of. 

But no... I don't really pace around. I just sort of sit in that chair and watch the wall until it's time to sleep.

Well, yeah, I have. The depression part has been with me for about a year and two months now. It started not long after the move. Moving is just... it takes it out of you, you know? I packed everything myself. I got all these boxes from the back of a grocery store down the street. Mostly banana boxes. They're the best for moving because they have those thick double walls and handles cut right into the sides. You just have to put a flat piece of cardboard over the hole in the bottom so your things don't fall out. 

Did you know bananas are actually classified as berries? Botanically speaking, I mean. But strawberries aren't. It has to do with how the flower grows and where the seeds are located. The bananas we eat today, the Cavendish ones, they're actually all genetic clones of one single plant. The original bananas that people used to eat, the Gros Michel, they got completely wiped out by a soil fungus back in the fifties. Panama disease, it was called. That's why artificial banana candy tastes so different from real bananas today—the flavor was modeled after the old type of banana that basically went extinct. It's strange to think about, isn't it? A whole type of fruit just vanishing off the face of the earth, and all we have left is the ghost of how it tasted in a piece of hard candy. 

But anyway... yeah, I've been feeling really down. Just sad all the time for the last year and two months, ever since I got to the new place.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, no... I don't really enjoy things much anymore. I used to look forward to fishing on Saturdays, or sitting down with a crossword puzzle and a good cup of coffee. I even liked showing the younger guys at work the right way to strip a floor without ruining the baseboards. But now... I mostly just let those things sit. They don't give me anything back, you know? 

Speaking of floor stripper, they changed the formula a few years ago. The old stuff used to smell like ammonia and pine, really strong, but it worked the first time you put it down. The new stuff is supposed to be eco-friendly. It comes in these big blue jugs with a green leaf on the label. But you have to let it sit for twenty minutes before you can even run the buffer over it. 

Did you know floor buffers actually spin counter-clockwise? Most people don't realize that. If you don't know how to handle the torque, the machine will just throw you right into the wall. You have to steer it by tilting the handle up and down, not by pushing it left and right. It's all about finding the center of gravity. It's a lot like riding a bicycle, really. Once you figure out the balance, you don't even have to think about it. 

I actually had a Schwinn bicycle when I was a kid. One of those classic ones with the banana seat and the high handlebars. They called them "ape hangers." Mine was cherry red with silver fenders. My dad bought it for me at a police auction. The police auction off all the stolen bikes they recover if nobody claims them after a year. It's a pretty good deal, really. You can get a perfectly good bike for ten dollars just because somebody forgot to register the serial number. 

But... yeah, the crosswords and the fishing. I just don't care about them anymore. I just don't have the energy for it.

Well, like I was just saying... yeah. I don't really care about the things I used to do. I mean, I used to love fishing on Saturdays. Just getting out there early. And doing the crossword puzzles in the paper while I had my morning coffee. I even liked my job, you know? Showing the younger guys the right way to strip a floor without ruining the baseboards. But now... I just let all that sit. It doesn't give me anything back anymore.

Speaking of the paper, though, they keep shrinking the size of it. The actual physical size of the newspaper. It's called broadsheet, the format they use, but over the last twenty years, they've been cutting the width down to save money on newsprint. Newsprint is actually a really terrible quality paper. It's highly acidic, which is why old newspapers turn yellow and brittle if you leave them in the sun or just keep them around too long. The acid in the wood pulp basically eats itself. 

If you want to preserve a newspaper clipping, you have to soak it in a mixture of club soda and milk of magnesia. The magnesium carbonate neutralizes the acid in the paper. My aunt taught me that. She used to cut out every single wedding announcement and obituary in the county and keep them in these big leather binders. She had a whole room just full of binders. But she lived in this old Victorian house that had knob-and-tube wiring, which is incredibly dangerous by today's standards. The wires are just run through these ceramic tubes inside the walls, and the insulation is made of cloth. Cloth! Can you imagine? Mice love to chew on it, and then you just have bare, live wires sitting inside dry wooden walls. It's a miracle the whole place didn't go up in smoke. 

But, um... yeah. The fishing and the crosswords. I just don't have the interest anymore.

I just sort of... go flat, you know? Quiet. Even at work, getting started on my cleaning route, it feels like I'm pushing a loaded cart uphill. Speaking of carts, the one they gave me last week has this squeaky wheel. It's the front left one, and it just squeaks and squeaks every time I turn a corner down the C-wing hallway. I told my supervisor, Frank, about it, but he just said to put some WD-40 on it. But WD-40 doesn't fix a bent axle, does it? I used to fix up old bicycles when I was taking some classes at the community college years ago, so I know a bent axle when I see one. Anyway, yeah, just... flat and quiet. That's how I feel.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this way, like you're just going flat and quiet?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... it's been a while now. I'd say it's been building up for about a year and five months. Right around the time I had to move out of my old apartment. I really liked that neighborhood, too. There was this little bakery on the corner that made the best sourdough bread. The guy who ran it, Mr. Henderson, he used to give me the day-old loaves for half price. He had this old golden retriever that just slept by the door all day. Good dog. But then the rent went up, and I had to pack everything. Packing is the worst, especially when you've got a lot of books. I have boxes and boxes of history books. Did you know the Romans used to use crushed oyster shells in their concrete? Makes it last forever. But yeah, ever since I had to leave that place and the neighborhood... that's when this whole flat feeling really started settling in.\n\nDoctor: Do you still find pleasure in activities that you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Not really, no. I used to look forward to things, you know? Like going fishing on Saturdays. I used to go down to the reservoir early in the morning. Had this lucky green and silver lure that my grandfather gave me. He worked on the railroads, actually. Laid track all the way across the state back in the thirties. He used to say you could tell a man's character by how he swung a hammer. He had these massive hands, just covered in callouses from years of steel work. \n\nBut anyway, fishing... or even just sitting down with a crossword puzzle and a good cup of coffee. I always used a pen for the crosswords. My dad thought that was showing off, using a pen instead of a pencil, but I just liked how the ink looked on the newspaper. Did you know the first crossword puzzle was published in 1913? A guy named Arthur Wynne invented it. It was diamond-shaped originally, not a square. \n\nBut yeah... I used to like doing those, or even just showing the younger guys at work some tricks for stripping a floor without leaving swirl marks. You have to overlap your passes just right. Now, though... I don't know. I mostly just let all those things sit. I don't even get the paper anymore. I just don't bother because... well, none of it gives me anything back anymore.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever thought about harming yourself or wished you were dead?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't have some big plan or anything like that to hurt myself. But... a lot of mornings, I wake up and just think it might be easier if I didn't wake up at all. \n\nI have this alarm clock that goes off at 4:30 AM every day. It's one of those old heavy metal ones with the twin bells on top. I found it at a garage sale on Elm Street a few years back. The lady selling it had this incredible collection of vintage salt and pepper shakers out on her porch. Hundreds of them, shaped like everything from farm animals to little astronauts. She said her husband started collecting them in the sixties, right around the time of the Apollo missions. Did you know the Apollo 11 astronauts actually ate bacon squares in space? They had to compress all the food so it wouldn't crumble and float into the instruments. \n\nAnyway, the clock is incredibly loud, which you need when you're working the early shift and have to get the floors buffed before the office staff comes in. But lately, when that bell rings... I just lie there and wish the ringing didn't matter because I wasn't here. And honestly... having that thought, just wanting to not wake up... it scares me enough to actually say it out loud to you right now.\n\nDoctor: Do you find yourself moving or speaking more slowly than you used to?\n\nPatient: Well, I don't... I haven't really noticed anything like that, moving slow or talking slow. I mean, I'm fifty-nine, so I guess my knees aren't what they used to be when I was playing softball in the church league. I played first base for a long time. We had these bright yellow jerseys. Terrible color, really. They attracted every gnat and mosquito in the park when the lights came on. The guy who ordered them, Frank... he thought yellow would make us look intimidating, like hornets or something. But we mostly just looked like a bunch of bananas running around the field. Frank was a plumber, actually. He told me once that copper pipes can last for fifty years if the water isn't too acidic. It's fascinating how things break down from the inside out without you even seeing it. But no, to answer your question... I don't think I'm moving any slower than normal. I just sort of do what I have to do.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost any weight recently?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I suppose I have. My work pants have been hanging a lot looser than they used to. I have to pull my belt in an extra notch or two. It's one of those braided leather belts, you know? I bought it at a craft fair down by the river maybe ten years ago. The guy making them was using this old-fashioned leather punch, just hammering away at his stall. He had a whole setup with different dyes and stamps. He told me that true leather working is all about the moisture content of the hide. If it's too dry, it cracks, but if it's too wet, it won't hold the impression. He was from out west somewhere, Montana maybe. Did you know Montana has the largest migratory elk herd in the nation? I saw a documentary about it once. They travel for hundreds of miles every year, just following the grass as the snow melts. \n\nBut anyway... about the weight. I just... I haven't been eating much. Most days food just tastes like cardboard to me. So I end up skipping meals, or I'll just eat a few crackers when I get home after my shift. I used to make a nice meatloaf on Sundays, but now... I just don't have the stomach for it.\n\nDoctor: Do you often feel guilty about things that have happened in your life?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I do. All the time, really. I keep thinking about how I failed everybody when I lost my old place and just... couldn't keep my life together. It's like this heavy weight, you know? Like if the church pantry is short on canned goods, or if one of the guys on the night shift misses a hallway, somehow I feel like that's on me, too. \n\nSpeaking of the church pantry, they used to have this enormous chest freezer down in the basement. One of those old white ones with the lid that weighed a ton. We used to store all the frozen turkeys in there around Thanksgiving. I remember one year, the compressor went out right before the holiday. It made this awful grinding noise, sounded like a garbage truck backing up. The repairman who came out to fix it, he had this fascinating theory about how modern appliances are designed to fail after a certain number of years. Planned obsolescence, he called it. He said back in the fifties, they built things to last forever because they used solid steel and copper wiring. Now it's all plastic gears and microchips that fry if the power surges. \n\nHe was actually a really interesting guy. He used to build model airplanes in his spare time. The kind with the tiny little gas engines that you fly with remote controls. He told me he once spent six months building a scale model of a P-51 Mustang, painted the invasion stripes and everything. Did you know the P-51 was originally designed for the British, but it didn't really become famous until they put a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine in it? It completely changed the air war over Europe. \n\nBut... yeah, the guilt. It just sort of sits there in my chest. I just feel like everything that goes wrong is somehow my fault, even when it doesn't make sense.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling restless or fidgety, or have you noticed yourself pacing back and forth more often than usual?\n\nPatient: Well, no... I haven't really noticed myself pacing or feeling fidgety. I'm usually pretty still, to be honest. Mostly I just sit in my chair when I get home. It's one of those recliners, you know, the kind with the lever on the side that always sticks a little bit. I bought it second-hand from a guy who was moving to Florida. He said he couldn't take it with him because the humidity down there ruins upholstery. \n\nHe was actually moving to Sarasota. Did you know Sarasota has some of the finest white sand beaches in the world? It's because the sand is made of pure quartz that washed down from the Appalachian Mountains millions of years ago. It stays cool even in the hot sun because it reflects the light. The guy told me he was going to buy a metal detector and just walk the beaches looking for lost jewelry. People lose so many rings and watches in the water because the cold ocean shrinks their fingers. \n\nHe showed me this old silver coin he found once in a park up here. A Mercury dime, from 1942. They're actually mostly silver, not like the coins we have now. The government stopped making silver coins for regular circulation back in 1964 because the silver was worth more than the face value of the coin. It's funny how value changes like that, isn't it? Something that's just a dime one day is suddenly worth a lot more just because of what it's made of. \n\nBut no... I don't really pace around. I just sort of sit in that chair and watch the wall until it's time to sleep.\n\nDoctor: Have you had periods in your life where you felt extremely sad or depressed for a long time?\n\nPatient: Well, yeah, I have. The depression part has been with me for about a year and two months now. It started not long after the move. Moving is just... it takes it out of you, you know? I packed everything myself. I got all these boxes from the back of a grocery store down the street. Mostly banana boxes. They're the best for moving because they have those thick double walls and handles cut right into the sides. You just have to put a flat piece of cardboard over the hole in the bottom so your things don't fall out. \n\nDid you know bananas are actually classified as berries? Botanically speaking, I mean. But strawberries aren't. It has to do with how the flower grows and where the seeds are located. The bananas we eat today, the Cavendish ones, they're actually all genetic clones of one single plant. The original bananas that people used to eat, the Gros Michel, they got completely wiped out by a soil fungus back in the fifties. Panama disease, it was called. That's why artificial banana candy tastes so different from real bananas today—the flavor was modeled after the old type of banana that basically went extinct. It's strange to think about, isn't it? A whole type of fruit just vanishing off the face of the earth, and all we have left is the ghost of how it tasted in a piece of hard candy. \n\nBut anyway... yeah, I've been feeling really down. Just sad all the time for the last year and two months, ever since I got to the new place.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy things you used to, or has your interest in them decreased over time?\n\nPatient: Well, no... I don't really enjoy things much anymore. I used to look forward to fishing on Saturdays, or sitting down with a crossword puzzle and a good cup of coffee. I even liked showing the younger guys at work the right way to strip a floor without ruining the baseboards. But now... I mostly just let those things sit. They don't give me anything back, you know? \n\nSpeaking of floor stripper, they changed the formula a few years ago. The old stuff used to smell like ammonia and pine, really strong, but it worked the first time you put it down. The new stuff is supposed to be eco-friendly. It comes in these big blue jugs with a green leaf on the label. But you have to let it sit for twenty minutes before you can even run the buffer over it. \n\nDid you know floor buffers actually spin counter-clockwise? Most people don't realize that. If you don't know how to handle the torque, the machine will just throw you right into the wall. You have to steer it by tilting the handle up and down, not by pushing it left and right. It's all about finding the center of gravity. It's a lot like riding a bicycle, really. Once you figure out the balance, you don't even have to think about it. \n\nI actually had a Schwinn bicycle when I was a kid. One of those classic ones with the banana seat and the high handlebars. They called them \"ape hangers.\" Mine was cherry red with silver fenders. My dad bought it for me at a police auction. The police auction off all the stolen bikes they recover if nobody claims them after a year. It's a pretty good deal, really. You can get a perfectly good bike for ten dollars just because somebody forgot to register the serial number. \n\nBut... yeah, the crosswords and the fishing. I just don't care about them anymore. I just don't have the energy for it.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like you've lost interest in activities you once found enjoyable?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying... yeah. I don't really care about the things I used to do. I mean, I used to love fishing on Saturdays. Just getting out there early. But now... I just let all that sit. It doesn't give me anything back anymore.\n\nSpeaking of the paper, though, they keep shrinking the size of it. The actual physical size of the newspaper. It's called broadsheet, the format they use, but over the last twenty years, they've been cutting the width down to save money on newsprint. Newsprint is actually a really terrible quality paper. It's highly acidic, which is why old newspapers turn yellow and brittle if you leave them in the sun or just keep them around too long. The acid in the wood pulp basically eats itself. \n\nIf you want to preserve a newspaper clipping, you have to soak it in a mixture of club soda and milk of magnesia. The magnesium carbonate neutralizes the acid in the paper. My aunt taught me that. She used to cut out every single wedding announcement and obituary in the county and keep them in these big leather binders. She had a whole room just full of binders. But she lived in this old Victorian house that had knob-and-tube wiring, which is incredibly dangerous by today's standards. The wires are just run through these ceramic tubes inside the walls, and the insulation is made of cloth. Cloth! Can you imagine? Slower? I don't know... I haven't really noticed my thoughts being slow, exactly. If anything, sometimes they just feel a little stuck, I guess? Or maybe I'm just tired. I've been sleeping a lot more since the move. 

Actually, the new place has these really heavy blackout curtains left over from the previous tenant. They're that thick, velvety material that hotels use. Hotels use them because they have to accommodate people on all different sleep schedules, like pilots and flight attendants. Did you know flight attendants have a strict limit on how many hours they can fly in a month? The FAA regulates it because of fatigue. Fatigue at high altitudes is actually worse because the cabin pressure is only equivalent to about 8,000 feet above sea level. So your blood oxygen level is lower the whole time you're up there. 

That's why tomato juice tastes better on airplanes. It's a real thing! The lower pressure and the dry air in the cabin actually numb your taste buds, specifically for sweet and salty flavors. But umami flavors, like in tomatoes and mushrooms, stay perfectly strong. So airlines go through thousands of gallons of tomato juice and Bloody Mary mix every year because people crave it in the air, even if they never drink it on the ground. It's funny how our bodies react to different environments without us even realizing it. Like how your ears pop when you drive up a mountain.

Well, the sadness... that depression part of it has been with me for about a year and two months, I'd say. It started up not long after the move. 

Moving is just... it's such a massive hassle. I rented one of those U-Haul trucks, the 15-foot ones with the little overhang above the cab. They call it "Mom's Attic," but really it's just a way to maximize cargo volume without extending the wheelbase of the chassis. It completely ruins the aerodynamics of the truck, though. The drag coefficient on a standard box truck is terrible. It's basically like driving a brick through a wind tunnel. That's why all the big semi-trucks you see on the highway have those curved fiberglass fairings on the roof now. They deflect the wind up and over the trailer, which saves the trucking companies thousands of gallons of diesel fuel every year. 

Diesel engines are actually really fascinating. Most people don't know this, but they don't use spark plugs at all. They rely entirely on the heat of compression to ignite the fuel inside the cylinder. Rudolf Diesel invented the engine back in the 1890s, and he originally designed it to run on peanut oil. He wanted it to be an engine for independent craftsmen and farmers, not just big oil industries. Can you imagine? If we had stuck with his original plan, the whole interstate system would just smell like roasting peanuts all day instead of heavy exhaust. 

But, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. The sadness. Yeah, about a year and two months. Right after I moved into the new place.

Before this one? No, I don't think so. I don't remember ever having anything like this that just lasted a month or two. It's really just been this one long stretch. 

Two months is a weird measure of time, anyway. It's usually about sixty days, unless February gets in the middle of it. February always throws the math off. Did you know the whole reason we have leap years is because it actually takes the Earth 365 point two four two two days to orbit the sun? It's not a clean quarter of a day. That's why the Gregorian calendar has that weird rule where leap years happen every four years, but they skip years that are divisible by 100, unless they're also divisible by 400. So the year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 wasn't. 

Pope Gregory XIII had to introduce that rule back in the 1580s because the old Julian calendar was drifting completely out of sync with the seasons. By the time they finally fixed it, they had to just delete ten days from October. People literally went to sleep on October 4th and woke up on October 15th. Can you imagine the payroll issues that would cause today? The union would have an absolute fit if the school district just deleted ten days from a pay period. When I first started with the district, they messed up my timesheet and shorted me just two days, and it took three months of paperwork to get the back pay. The bureaucracy is just staggering. 

But, um... what was the question? Oh, right. Shorter times feeling like this. No, I haven't had that. Just this one long one since the move.

Before this? No, I don't think I've ever felt this low before. It's like I've just hit the absolute bare floor. 

Speaking of bare floors, stripping the tile at the school is probably the hardest part of the summer maintenance schedule. Most people think you just mop some soap on it, but commercial floor stripper is highly alkaline. It usually has a pH around 13 or 14, which is basically like working with straight lye. It chemically breaks down the zinc cross-links in the old acrylic finish. That's why you have to flood the floor and let it dwell for ten minutes. But if you let it dry out, it turns into this concrete-like sludge that is completely impossible to get off. And then you have to rinse the whole thing with a chemical neutralizer before you can even think about putting the new wax down. If the floor's pH is too high, the new finish won't adhere properly and it just powders off as soon as the kids start walking on it. 

Kids destroy those floors in about a week anyway. Especially with those shoes that have the little wheels hidden in the heels. I don't even know how those are still allowed in a public building. It's a massive liability issue. If a kid slips and cracks their head on a cinderblock wall, the district's insurance premiums would just skyrocket. The insurance actuaries calculate risk down to the absolute penny for those municipal policies, so they're always sending inspectors to check our wet floor signs and mat placements. 

But, um... sorry, my mind is wandering again. What did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling depressed before. No, I haven't. I've never had anything like this happen before the current stretch.

They don't give me anything back, you know? \n\nSpeaking of floor stripper, they changed the formula a few years ago. The old stuff used to smell like ammonia and pine, really strong, but it worked the first time you put it down. The new stuff is supposed to be eco-friendly. No, I don't think so. I really haven't ever felt this way before this whole thing started. I mean, sure, everyone gets sad sometimes, but not like this.

No, I... I really don't think so. Like I said, this is the first time I've ever been stuck down in a hole like this. I haven't had multiple times of feeling this way, just this one long stretch right now. 

It's funny how time stretches out when you're just sitting in it. Speaking of stretching time, did you know that because of time dilation, the astronauts on the International Space Station actually age slightly slower than people on Earth? It's a fraction of a second, but it's real. It has to do with Einstein's theory of relativity and how gravity warps spacetime. The closer you are to a massive object, the slower time moves. 

I was watching this documentary about black holes the other night when I couldn't sleep. The gravity of a black hole is so intense that not even light can escape it once it passes the event horizon. If you were falling into a black hole, someone watching from the outside would see you slow down and eventually just freeze in place forever, but from your perspective, time would just be moving normally until you were spaghettified by the tidal forces. That's the actual scientific term they use—spaghettification. Because the gravity pulling on your feet would be so much stronger than the gravity pulling on your head that you'd just get stretched out into a long string of atoms. 

It makes you wonder what happens to all the information that falls in. Stephen Hawking spent years arguing about the information paradox. If quantum mechanics says information can't be destroyed, but general relativity says a black hole eventually evaporates and disappears, where does all that stuff go? 

Anyway... I'm sorry, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Uh, what were we just saying? Oh, right. More than one episode. No, just this one. Just this current time.

The acid in the wood pulp basically eats itself. \n\nIf you want to preserve a newspaper clipping, you have to soak it in a mixture of club soda and milk of magnesia. The magnesium carbonate neutralizes the acid in the paper. My aunt taught me that. She used to cut out every single wedding announcement and obituary in the county and keep them in these big leather binders. She had a whole room just full of binders. But she lived in this old Victorian house that had knob-and-tube wiring, which is incredibly dangerous by today's standards. The wires are just run through these ceramic tubes inside the walls, and the insulation is made of cloth. Cloth! Can you imagine? Mice love to chew on it, and then you just have bare, live wires sitting inside dry wooden walls. It's a miracle the whole place didn't go up in smoke. \n\nBut, um... yeah. The fishing and the crosswords. I just don't have the interest anymore.\n\nDoctor: Do you feel like your thoughts are slower than they used to be?\n\nPatient: Slower? I don't know... I haven't really noticed my thoughts being slow, exactly. If anything, sometimes they just feel a little stuck, I guess? Or maybe I'm just tired. I've been sleeping a lot more since the move. \n\nActually, the new place has these really heavy blackout curtains left over from the previous tenant. They're that thick, velvety material that hotels use. Hotels use them because they have to accommodate people on all different sleep schedules, like pilots and flight attendants. Did you know flight attendants have a strict limit on how many hours they can fly in a month? The FAA regulates it because of fatigue. Fatigue at high altitudes is actually worse because the cabin pressure is only equivalent to about 8,000 feet above sea level. So your blood oxygen level is lower the whole time you're up there. \n\nThat's why tomato juice tastes better on airplanes. It's a real thing! The lower pressure and the dry air in the cabin actually numb your taste buds, specifically for sweet and salty flavors. But umami flavors, like in tomatoes and mushrooms, stay perfectly strong. So airlines go through thousands of gallons of tomato juice and Bloody Mary mix every year because people crave it in the air, even if they never drink it on the ground. It's funny how our bodies react to different environments without us even realizing it. Like how your ears pop when you drive up a mountain. \n\nBut um... what were you asking? Oh, right. My thoughts. No, I wouldn't say they're slower. I just... I haven't really noticed anything like that.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling this persistent sadness and loss of interest in activities?\n\nPatient: Well, the sadness... that depression part of it has been with me for about a year and two months, I'd say. It started up not long after the move. \n\nMoving is just... it's such a massive hassle. I rented one of those U-Haul trucks, the 15-foot ones with the little overhang above the cab. They call it \"Mom's Attic,\" but really it's just a way to maximize cargo volume without extending the wheelbase of the chassis. It completely ruins the aerodynamics of the truck, though. The drag coefficient on a standard box truck is terrible. It's basically like driving a brick through a wind tunnel. That's why all the big semi-trucks you see on the highway have those curved fiberglass fairings on the roof now. They deflect the wind up and over the trailer, which saves the trucking companies thousands of gallons of diesel fuel every year. \n\nDiesel engines are actually really fascinating. Most people don't know this, but they don't use spark plugs at all. They rely entirely on the heat of compression to ignite the fuel inside the cylinder. Rudolf Diesel invented the engine back in the 1890s, and he originally designed it to run on peanut oil. He wanted it to be an engine for independent craftsmen and farmers, not just big oil industries. Can you imagine? If we had stuck with his original plan, the whole interstate system would just smell like roasting peanuts all day instead of heavy exhaust. \n\nBut, um... what was I saying? Oh, right. The sadness. Yeah, about a year and two months. Right after I moved into the new place.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any episodes of depression that lasted for less than two months before this current period?\n\nPatient: Before this one? No, I don't think so. I don't remember ever having anything like this that just lasted a month or two. It's really just been this one long stretch. \n\nTwo months is a weird measure of time, anyway. It's usually about sixty days, unless February gets in the middle of it. February always throws the math off. Did you know the whole reason we have leap years is because it actually takes the Earth 365 point two four two two days to orbit the sun? It's not a clean quarter of a day. That's why the Gregorian calendar has that weird rule where leap years happen every four years, but they skip years that are divisible by 100, unless they're also divisible by 400. So the year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 wasn't. \n\nPope Gregory XIII had to introduce that rule back in the 1580s because the old Julian calendar was drifting completely out of sync with the seasons. By the time they finally fixed it, they had to just delete ten days from October. People literally went to sleep on October 4th and woke up on October 15th. Can you imagine the payroll issues that would cause today? The union would have an absolute fit if the school district just deleted ten days from a pay period. When I first started with the district, they messed up my timesheet and shorted me just two days, and it took three months of paperwork to get the back pay. The bureaucracy is just staggering. \n\nBut, um... what was the question? Oh, right. Shorter times feeling like this. No, I haven't had that. Just this one long one since the move.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt this low or depressed before this current period?\n\nPatient: Before this? No, I don't think I've ever felt this low before. It's like I've just hit the absolute bare floor. \n\nSpeaking of bare floors, stripping the tile at the school is probably the hardest part of the summer maintenance schedule. Most people think you just mop some soap on it, but commercial floor stripper is highly alkaline. It usually has a pH around 13 or 14, which is basically like working with straight lye. It chemically breaks down the zinc cross-links in the old acrylic finish. That's why you have to flood the floor and let it dwell for ten minutes. But if you let it dry out, it turns into this concrete-like sludge that is completely impossible to get off. If the floor's pH is too high, the new finish won't adhere properly and it just powders off as soon as the kids start walking on it. \n\nKids destroy those floors in about a week anyway. Especially with those shoes that have the little wheels hidden in the heels. I don't even know how those are still allowed in a public building. It's a massive liability issue. It's that pre-ground industrial stuff that comes in those giant silver foil bags. It's completely stale before you even open it because all the volatile aromatic compounds evaporate within hours of the beans being ground. Coffee beans are actually seeds, not beans, from the Coffea plant. The two main species are Arabica and Robusta. Robusta has almost twice the caffeine content and is much more disease-resistant, which is why they use it in all those cheap commercial blends, but it tastes like burnt rubber. Arabica is much sweeter and more complex, but it requires higher elevations to grow. The optimal altitude for growing Arabica is between 3,000 and 6,000 feet above sea level. \n\nThat's why the best coffee comes from places like the mountains of Colombia or Ethiopia. Ethiopia is actually where coffee was discovered. There's this legend about a goat herder named Kaldi who noticed his goats getting really energetic after eating the red berries from a certain bush. Just like the guy who invented the intermittent windshield wiper. The big auto companies completely stole his patent and he spent his whole life fighting them in court. Oh, right. Enjoying things. Yeah, I just don't get any enjoyment out of fishing or the crosswords or anything anymore. It's a fraction of a second, but it's real. It has to do with Einstein's theory of relativity and how gravity warps spacetime. The closer you are to a massive object, the slower time moves. \n\nI was watching this documentary about black holes the other night when I couldn't sleep. The gravity of a black hole is so intense that not even light can escape it once it passes the event horizon. If you were falling into a black hole, someone watching from the outside would see you slow down and eventually just freeze in place forever, but from your perspective, time would just be moving normally until you were spaghettified by the tidal forces. That's the actual scientific term they use—spaghettification. Because the gravity pulling on your feet would be so much stronger than the gravity pulling on your head that you'd just get stretched out into a long string of atoms. \n\nIt makes you wonder what happens to all the information that falls in. Stephen Hawking spent years arguing about the information paradox.
